OUTPUT FILES (written to wage_file_outputs <- "./processing_files/", which is created if it does not exist):
  Xtrain_500000_20.Rdata                           Xtrain, W, Y, weights_supplied, weights_dummy: random sample of 500,000 rows (occupation 23 levels, industry 20 levels)

  industry_mapping_full_description.Rdata, occupation_mapping_full_description.Rdata, variable_mappings.Rdata    numeric code -> description
  Supplementary_1_results.Rdata                    the list res: the counts behind the text and the tests
  Supplementary_1_tests.txt, Supplementary_1_session.txt    test results and session information
  Supplementary_1_figs/                            wage by code plots (only if fig_eval_flag)

FLAGS (set in the setup chunk):
  eval_flag      TRUE runs the processing chunks (needs the raw data and about 20 GB of memory). FALSE only knits the text.
  fig_eval_flag  TRUE writes the diagnostic plots to Supplementary_1_figs/.
  The chunks with eval=FALSE are old or exploratory code that is kept for reference (they are not run).

UNIT TESTS: chunks named tests_* call run_test("description", { testthat::expect_...() }). The results are listed by the last chunk and written to
  Supplementary_1_tests.txt. A failing test means that a number in the text, or an assumption of the later files, no longer holds.

PROGRESS: step("message") writes the time and a message to the console (stderr), so a long run shows where it is. rmarkdown prints a chunk label only when
  the chunk starts, so a slow load or a slow step looks like a hang.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width=6, fig.height=6, dpi=300,echo = FALSE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.pos = "H", out.extra = "")

# eval_flag: TRUE runs the processing chunks. FALSE knits only the text.
# fig_eval_flag: TRUE writes the diagnostic plots to Supplementary_1_figs/.
eval_flag <- TRUE
fig_eval_flag <- TRUE
if (!eval_flag) fig_eval_flag <- FALSE

test_log <- "Supplementary_1_tests.txt"
results_file <- "Supplementary_1_results.Rdata"
res <- list()   # the counts behind the text and the tests; saved at the end
test_results <- data.frame(test = character(), result = character(), detail = character(), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
run_test <- function(description, code) {
  detail <- tryCatch({ force(code); "" }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
  result <- if (identical(detail, "")) "PASS" else "FAIL"
  test_results[nrow(test_results) + 1, ] <<- c(description, result, detail)
  cat(sprintf("[%s] %s\n", result, description))
  if (result == "FAIL") cat("       ", detail, "\n")
  invisible(result == "PASS")
}
# progress messages go to stderr, which knitr does not capture, so they show on the console during a long run
step <- function(msg) cat(format(Sys.time(), "%H:%M:%S"), " ", msg, "\n", sep = "", file = stderr())

```

# the PUMS wage data. 

We take wage data from the 2018 American Community Survey by the US Census Bureau and using this we analyze the gender wage gap. See
@nafStudyingGenderWage2023, which inspired this work.

The PUMS (Public Use Microdata Area) data from the 2018 1-Year American Community Survey is obtained from the US Census
Bureau. The  API is described [here](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/data/developers/api-user-guide/api-guide.pdf).

The survey is sent to $\approx$ 3.5 million people annually and aims to give more up to date data than the official census that is carried out every
decade. The 2018 data set has 3,2140,539 anonymized data points for the 51 states and District of Columbia.  relevant for the salaries:

-  person's gender, age, race (AIAN, black, white, asian, mix, NHOPI, other), indicator of hispanic origin, state of residence, US citizenship
indicator (5 ordered levels), indicator whether the person is foreign-born
- person's marital status, number of own children in the same household and the number of family members in the same household
- for employed people we have annual salary earnings, number of weeks worked in a year and average number of hours worked per week
- for employed people we have employer type (government, non-profit company, for-profit company, self-employed), occupation (530 levels), industry
where the person works (271 levels) and the geographical unit where the person works (59 levels)
- statistical weight determined by the US Census Bureau which aims to correct sampling bias

Since we want to analyze the gender pay gap, we consider only employed people that
are at least 17 years of age, have worked full-time (at least 48 weeks in a year) and have worked at least 16 hours a
week on average. We also omit the self-employed persons, since they often report zero annual salary and the pay gap
there, if exists, cannot be called unfair as the salary is not determined by any employer. Since there are no missing
data which would need to be omitted, we finally end up with 1,061,763  data points. 

We scale the salary with the amount of time spent working (determined from the number of weeks worked and average
hours worked per week) to compute the logarithm of the hourly wages. The scaling with the time spent working used as 
full-time employed men spend on average 11\% more time working than women. The logarithmic
transformation is used since the salaries are very skewed (positively) and logarithmic wages show nice behavior.

## handling discrete and continuous variables

Table \ref{table:variables} shows the variables in the processed data. There is a mixture of continuous and discrete variables. 

- education had 23 levels. However, we mapped them to a continuous variable which we roughly take to be an approximation to years of schooling. See table \@ref(table:educationlevel)
- For some parts of the analysis we reduce the large number of levels of some of the categorical variables: 

   - for the occupation we use the group of 530 jobs into 20 categories provided in the SOC system (https://www.bls.gov/soc/), See table
\@ref(table:20industryCategories)
   - for the industry information we group the 271 possibilities in 23 categories as is done in the NIACS classification
(https://www.bls.gov/bls/naics.htm);
   - for the work place we group the 59 US states and foreign territories into 9 economic regions (including the "abroad" category), as determined by
   the Bureau of the Economic Analysis (https://apps.bea.gov/regional/docs/regions.cfm).

## the raw data

```{R rawdata, echo=TRUE, eval=eval_flag}
step("loading the raw data")
load(paste(wage_data_dir, "wage_data.Rdata", sep="")) # if you have the data local
step("raw data loaded")
dim(wage)# [1] 3214539      25
res$n_raw <- nrow(wage)
wage[1:4,1:8]
#     sex age  race hispanic_origin citizenship nativity       marital family_size 
#1   male   5 white              no           1   native never married           3 
#2   male  11 white              no           1   native never married           3 
#3 female  47 white              no           1   native      divorced           3 
#4   male  70 white              no           1   native       married           2 

which = rep(TRUE, nrow(wage))
which = which & (wage$age >= 17)
which = which & (wage$weeks_worked > 48)
which = which & (wage$hours_worked > 16)
which = which & (wage$employment_status == 'employed')
which = which & (wage$employer != 'self-employed')
which[is.na(which)] = FALSE
table(which)
res$n_selected <- sum(which)
#   which
#  FALSE    TRUE 
#2142673 1071866 

step("selecting the rows")
wage$industry_description<- unlist(wage$industry_description)

data = wage[which, ]  #1071866      25
sum(is.na(data)) #0
colSums(is.na(data))

# OK there was a problem here. The value "-1" was used by the "children" variable to denote a missing value.
sum(data$children==-1) #[1] 10103
res$n_children_missing <- sum(data$children==-1)
step("replacing the missing-value code -1 by NA and dropping those rows")
# (done column by column on the numeric columns: data[data == -1] on the whole data frame builds a 1,000,000 x 25 matrix and is very slow
#  when there are list columns)
for (v in names(data)[vapply(data, is.numeric, NA)]) data[[v]][data[[v]] == -1] <- NA
keep <- complete.cases(data[!vapply(data, is.list, NA)])
data <- data[keep, ]
rownames(data) = 1:nrow(data)
dim(data) # 1061763      25

sum(data$industry == "", na.rm=TRUE)  # How many empty strings?
# 0
sum(is.na(data$industry))              # How many true NAs?
# 0
head(levels(data$industry))
#[1] ""     "111"  "112"  "1133" "113M" "114" 
#No actual data rows have industry == "" (that's why the sum is 0)
# But "" exists as an unused factor level

data$industry <- droplevels(data$industry)

table(unlist(lapply(data,class)))
which(lapply(data,class)=="character") #education 
which(lapply(data,class)=="list") #occupation_description   industry_description 
which(lapply(data,class)=="factor") #sex  race   hispanic_origin nativity  marital state employment_status  occupation industry  employer  place_of_work   economic_region 
which(lapply(data,class)=="numeric") #age citizenship family_size children education_level english_level  salary  hours_worked   weeks_worked    weight 

head(levels(data$industry))

data$occupation_description[(which(data$occupation=="55-9830"))][1]
#[1] "Military, rank not specified"

data$occupation_description[(which(data$occupation=="999920"))][1]
#NULL

# Note: Using occupation_description from PUMS data rather than 
# 2018-occupation-code-list-and-crosswalk.xlsx because:
# 1. PUMS data includes military occupations (55-9830) not in crosswalk
# 2. Some codes in crosswalk (999920) don't appear in actual data
# droplevels() removes unused codes like 999920

data$occupation <- droplevels(data$occupation)
data$industry <- droplevels(data$industry)
dim(data) #[1] 1061763      25
res$n_final <- nrow(data)
step("the data set is ready")

```

```{r tests_data, echo=FALSE, eval=eval_flag, results='hide'}
run_test("raw data: 3,214,539 rows and 25 columns", {
  expect_equal(res$n_raw, 3214539)
  expect_equal(ncol(wage), 25)
})
run_test("selection: 1,071,866 people are employed full time (age >= 17, weeks > 48, hours > 16, not self-employed)", {
  expect_equal(res$n_selected, 1071866)
})
run_test("missing values: 10,103 people with children == -1 (the missing-value code) are dropped, leaving 1,061,763", {
  expect_equal(res$n_children_missing, 10103)
  expect_equal(res$n_final, 1061763)
  expect_equal(nrow(data), 1061763)
})
run_test("data: no missing values, no -1 codes, and the selection rules hold in every row", {
  nl <- data[!vapply(data, is.list, NA)]
  expect_equal(sum(is.na(nl)), 0)
  expect_equal(sum(data$children == -1), 0)
  expect_true(all(data$age >= 17))
  expect_true(all(data$weeks_worked > 48))
  expect_true(all(data$hours_worked > 16))
  expect_true(all(data$employment_status == "employed"))
  expect_true(all(data$employer != "self-employed"))
  expect_true(all(data$salary > 0))
})
run_test("data: both genders are present, occupation has 529 levels and industry 269 (no unused levels)", {
  expect_equal(sort(unique(as.character(data$sex))), c("female", "male"))
  expect_equal(nlevels(data$occupation), 529)
  expect_equal(nlevels(data$industry), 269)
  expect_false("" %in% levels(data$industry))
})
run_test("data: the occupation and industry descriptions are available for every row", {
  expect_equal(length(data$occupation_description), nrow(data))
  expect_equal(length(data$industry_description), nrow(data))
})
run_test("data: the 24 education levels are all used, and each one has a single education_level (years of schooling)", {
  expect_equal(length(unique(data$education)), 24)
  expect_equal(sum(table(data$education)), 1061763)
  expect_true(all(rowSums(table(data$education, data$education_level) > 0) == 1))
})
```

# set up Xtrain 

- with occupation reduced to 23 levels and industry reduced to 20 levels
- save as Xtrain_500000_20.Rdata
- not generating or using Xtest at the moment

```{R xtrain_setup, echo=FALSE, eval=eval_flag}
step("setting up Xtrain (23 occupation and 20 industry levels)")
data$log_wage = log(data$salary / (data$weeks_worked * data$hours_worked))
X  <- data[,c(
    'sex',
  'log_wage',
  'age',
  'race',
  'hispanic_origin',
  'citizenship',
  'nativity', 
  'marital',
  'family_size',
  'children',
  'education_level',
  'english_level',
  'economic_region',
  'weight'
)]


X$occupation  <- unlist(lapply(as.character(data$occupation), function(s){return(substr(s, 1, 2))})) #returns the first 2 characters of the occupation code i.e
#  13-2011 becomes 13
X$occupation  <- as.factor(X$occupation) #reduced occupation 530 levels to 23 levels

#add  industry and reduce the levels from 271 to 20

# Industry codes are 2 digits long. The first digit represents the sector, and the second digit represents the subsector.
# We will use the first digit to reduce the number of levels from 271 to 20.
# We will also combine some subsectors that are similar. For example, we will combine subsectors 32 and 33 into sector 31.
# We will also combine subsectors 42 and 44 into sector 41, subsectors 45 and 44 into sector 44, subsectors 49 and 48 into sector 48, and subsectors 92 and 91 into sector 91.

X$industry  <- unlist(lapply(as.character(data$industry), function(s){return(substr(s, 1, 2))})) #strip the classification to the first 2 numbers. This reduces it to 26 categories
X$industry[X$industry %in% c('32', '33', '3M')] = '31'
X$industry[X$industry %in% c('42')] = '41'
X$industry[X$industry %in% c('45', '4M')] = '44'
X$industry[X$industry %in% c('49')] = '48'
X$industry[X$industry %in% c('92')] = '91'
X$industry  <- as.factor(X$industry)

```



```{R xtrain_save, echo=FALSE, eval=eval_flag}
# process the other variables

X$citizenship <-as.factor(X$citizenship)
X$sex <-as.factor(X$sex)

#
#X$english_level <- as.factor(X$english_level) #is this correct. No treat english_level as a numeric variable (years of schooling)
X$economic_region <-as.factor(X$economic_region)

#X$children[X$children == -1 ]  <- NA # -1 was a missing value code. will rCausalMGM handle missing values? they are dropped
# not nned for this any longer. Fixed earlier

X <-droplevels(X[X$economic_region !="Abroad",]) #no problem here but in Xtrain,Xtest we get Categorical: <5 samples in a category
table(unlist(lapply(X,class)))
# factor numeric 
#     9       7 



#set.seed(123)
set.seed(124)
train_idx = sample(1:nrow(X), 500000, replace = FALSE)
test_idx = sample((1:nrow(X))[-train_idx], 500000, replace = FALSE)


Xtrain=X[train_idx,]
Xtrain <-droplevels(Xtrain[Xtrain$economic_region !="Abroad",]) #Categorical: <5 samples in a category
sum(is.na(Xtrain)) #0

Xtrain <- Xtrain[complete.cases(Xtrain),]
Y <- Xtrain$log_wage
W <- Xtrain$sex
head(Xtrain$sex)
#[1] male   male   male   female female male    Levels: female male
W <- as.numeric(W) -1
head(W) #[1] 1 1 1 0 0 1
Xtrain <- Xtrain[,-c(1:2)]

# in some grf functions 
#male    (W = 1) is called "treated" 
#female  (W = 0) is called "control"

table(unlist(lapply(Xtrain,class)))
# factor numeric 
#      8       6 
names(Xtrain)
# [1] "age"             "race"            "hispanic_origin" "citizenship"     "nativity"        "marital"         "family_size"     "children"       
# [9] "education_level" "english_level"   "economic_region" "weight"          "occupation"      "industry"       


dim(Xtrain) #[1]  500000     13 # 14 with the weight variable
class(Xtrain) #[1] "data.frame"

weights_supplied <-Xtrain$weight
weights_dummy <- rep(1,length(weights_supplied))
Xtrain <- Xtrain %>% 
  select(-weight) 
    
save(Xtrain ,W,Y, weights_supplied , weights_dummy , file=paste(wage_file_outputs, "Xtrain_500000_20.Rdata", sep=""))

#save(Xtrain ,W,Y, file="./script9/Xtrain_500000_industry.Rdata")   not used  


dim(Xtrain)
#[1]  500000     13
table(unlist(lapply(Xtrain, class)))
# factor numeric 
#      8       5 
#
#numeric age family_size children education_level english_level
#factor  race  hispanic_origin citizenship nativity marital economic_region occupation industry
res$xtrain <- list(dim = dim(Xtrain), n_factor = sum(sapply(Xtrain, is.factor)), n_numeric = sum(sapply(Xtrain, is.numeric)),
                   levels = sapply(Xtrain[sapply(Xtrain, is.factor)], nlevels), train_idx = length(train_idx))
step("Xtrain saved")

```

```{r tests_xtrain, echo=FALSE, eval=eval_flag, results='hide'}
run_test("Xtrain: 500,000 rows, 13 covariates (8 factors, 5 numeric), no missing values", {
  expect_equal(dim(Xtrain), c(500000, 13))
  expect_equal(sum(sapply(Xtrain, is.factor)), 8)
  expect_equal(sum(sapply(Xtrain, is.numeric)), 5)
  expect_equal(sum(is.na(Xtrain)), 0)
})
run_test("Xtrain: occupation has 23 levels, industry 20 and economic_region 8 (the region Abroad is dropped)", {
  expect_equal(nlevels(Xtrain$occupation), 23)
  expect_equal(nlevels(Xtrain$industry), 20)
  expect_equal(nlevels(Xtrain$economic_region), 8)
  expect_false("Abroad" %in% levels(Xtrain$economic_region))
})
run_test("Xtrain: W is 0/1, Y is finite, the weights are positive and the lengths agree", {
  expect_true(all(W %in% c(0, 1)))
  expect_true(all(is.finite(Y)))
  expect_true(all(weights_supplied > 0))
  expect_equal(length(Y), nrow(Xtrain)); expect_equal(length(W), nrow(Xtrain)); expect_equal(length(weights_supplied), nrow(Xtrain))
})
run_test("Xtrain: the saved file reloads with the same objects", {
  e <- new.env(); load(paste0(wage_file_outputs, "Xtrain_500000_20.Rdata"), e)
  expect_setequal(ls(e), c("Xtrain", "W", "Y", "weights_supplied", "weights_dummy"))
  expect_equal(dim(e$Xtrain), c(500000, 13))
})
```

#  set up Xtrain_ordered_numeric 

- one-hot-encoding  may be a poor choice
- explicitly emulate the effect of respect.unordered.factors="order"
- with occupation have the full description and the 2018 SOC code (530 levels) and industry have the full description and the 2018 NAICS code (271 levels)
- this code is the alternative code for setting up the data with 530 occupation levels and 271 industry levels
- we ran into an issue here
   
   - the training and test data are being created from the original data frame X where these variables are factor
   - For Xtrain we ordered factors by mean response and converted to numeric
   - For Xtest we did the same process independently
   - This means the ordering and thus numeric coding could be different between train and test

- To fix this, we should, do the ordering and numeric conversion on the full dataset X first   Then split into train and test
- however, not creating or using Xtest_ordered_numeric at the moment

```{r order_levels, echo=FALSE, eval=eval_flag}
# now we do it this way
order_levels_by_mean_response <- function(df, Y, factor_col) {
  # Calculate mean response for each level
  mean_response <- tapply(Y, df[[factor_col]], mean)
  
  # Order levels by mean response
  ordered_levels <- names(sort(mean_response))
  
  # Convert factor to ordered factor
  df[[factor_col]] <- factor(df[[factor_col]], levels = ordered_levels)
  
  return(df)
}

X_ordered <- X
for (col in c("race", "citizenship", "marital", "economic_region", "occupation" ,"industry")) {
  X_ordered <- order_levels_by_mean_response(X_ordered , X_ordered$log_wage , col)
}
```

# Variable Mapping Creation

For 

When we emulated `r respect.unordered.factors="order"`
to make Xtrain_ordered_numeric
we  have made new levels (or numeric codes) for all of the variables 
`r c("race", "citizenship", "marital", "economic_region", "occupation" ,"industry") `
This does not matter if we are not going to interpret their levels -- but we  will be doing that for some variables.   We need to make a map of numeric codes to variable level descriptors for all of these variables




```{verbatim, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
Most common PUMS English proficiency coding:

    0: "Not at all" (no English)
    1: "Not well"
    2: "Well"
    3: "Very well"
    4: "Speaks only English"
```

```{R mappings, echo=FALSE, eval=eval_flag}
step("creating the mappings")
# ============================================================
# COMPLETE MAPPING CREATION FOR ALL CATEGORICAL VARIABLES
# ============================================================

library(dplyr)

# ============================================================
# PART 1: CREATE MAPPINGS
# ============================================================

create_mapping <- function(data_orig, X_factor, X_numeric, var_name, 
                          code_col = NULL, desc_col = NULL) {
  
  # Create contingency table between factor and numeric versions
  contingency <- table(
    original = X_factor[[var_name]],
    new = X_numeric[[var_name]]
  )
  
  # Extract mapping: which original code maps to which new numeric code
  mapping_df <- as.data.frame.table(contingency) %>%
    filter(Freq > 0) %>%
    select(original_code = original, new_code = new) %>%
    mutate(
      original_code = as.character(original_code),
      new_code = as.numeric(as.character(new_code))
    ) %>%
    distinct()
  
  # Get the lookup from original data (if available)
  if (!is.null(code_col) && !is.null(desc_col)) {
    lookup <- data_orig %>%
      select(all_of(c(code_col, desc_col))) %>%
      rename(original_code = 1, description = 2) %>%
      # the description of the occupations is a list column in the raw data (one string per element):
      # make it a character vector, so that the mapping has plain character columns
      mutate(original_code = as.character(original_code),
             description = vapply(description, function(e) if (length(e) == 0) NA_character_ else as.character(e)[1],
                                  character(1))) %>%
      distinct()
  } else {
    # For variables without separate description columns
    # Use factor levels as both code and description
    lookup <- data.frame(
      original_code = as.character(levels(X_factor[[var_name]])),
      description = as.character(levels(X_factor[[var_name]])),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
  
  # Merge with descriptions
  mapping_final <- mapping_df %>%
    left_join(lookup, by = "original_code") %>%
    arrange(new_code)
  
  return(mapping_final)
}

# Create all mappings
cat("Creating mappings...\n")

# Industry mapping (269 original codes -> aggregated codes)

  X_numeric = X_ordered_numeric,
  var_name = "industry",

  desc_col = "industry_description"
)

# Occupation mapping (530 original codes -> aggregated codes)

  var_name = "occupation",
  code_col = "occupation",
  desc_col = "occupation_description"
)

# Race mapping
race_mapping <- create_mapping(
  data_orig = data,

  var_name = "race"
)

# Citizenship mapping

)

# Create citizenship descriptions lookup (since not in original data)
citizenship_descriptions <- data.frame(
  original_code = as.character(1:5),
  description = c(
    "Born in the U.S.",
    "Born in Puerto Rico, Guam, U.S. Virgin Islands, or Northern Marianas",
    "Born abroad of American parent(s)",
    "U.S. citizen by naturalization",
    "Not a U.S. citizen"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Update the citizenship mapping with proper descriptions

cat("All mappings created successfully!\n\n")

# ============================================================
# PART 2: UNIT TESTS FOR MAPPINGS
# ============================================================

cat(strrep("=", 60), "\n")
cat("Running unit tests...\n")
cat(strrep("=", 60), "\n")

# Test 1: Check that all mappings have required columns
test_mapping_structure <- function(mapping, name) {
  cat("\nTest 1 -", name, "structure:\n")
  
  required_cols <- c("original_code", "new_code", "description")
  has_cols <- all(required_cols %in% names(mapping))
  
  if (has_cols) {
    cat("  OK Has all required columns\n")
  } else {
    cat("  X FAILED: Missing columns:", 
        setdiff(required_cols, names(mapping)), "\n")
  }
  
  return(has_cols)
}

# Test 2: Check for NA values
test_mapping_nas <- function(mapping, name) {
  cat("\nTest 2 -", name, "NA values:\n")
  
  na_counts <- colSums(is.na(mapping))
  
  if (all(na_counts == 0)) {
    cat("  OK No NA values found\n")
    result <- TRUE
  } else {
    cat("  ! WARNING: Found NA values:\n")
    print(na_counts[na_counts > 0])
    result <- FALSE
  }
  
  return(result)
}

# Test 3: Check that new_codes are sequential starting from 1
test_sequential_codes <- function(mapping, name) {
  cat("\nTest 3 -", name, "sequential codes:\n")
  
  expected <- as.integer(1:max(mapping$new_code))
  actual <- as.integer(sort(unique(mapping$new_code)))
  
  if (identical(expected, actual)) {
    cat("  OK Sequential codes 1 to", max(mapping$new_code), "\n")
    result <- TRUE
  } else {
    cat("  X FAILED: Non-sequential codes\n")
    cat("    Expected: 1 to", max(mapping$new_code), "\n")
    cat("    Missing:", setdiff(expected, actual), "\n")
    cat("    Extra:", setdiff(actual, expected), "\n")
    result <- FALSE
  }
  
  return(result)
}

# Test 4: Check that wages increase with new_code
test_wage_ordering <- function(X_numeric, Y, var_name, name) {
  cat("\nTest 4 -", name, "wage ordering:\n")
  
  mean_wages <- tapply(Y, X_numeric[[var_name]], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  is_increasing <- all(diff(mean_wages) >= 0)
  
  if (is_increasing) {
    cat("  OK Wages increase with new_code\n")
  } else {
    cat("  ! WARNING: Wages do not always increase with new_code\n")
    decreases <- which(diff(mean_wages) < 0)
    cat("    Decreases at positions:", decreases, "\n")
  }
  
  return(is_increasing)
}

# Test 5: Check mapping coverage
test_mapping_coverage <- function(X_factor, mapping, var_name, name) {
  cat("\nTest 5 -", name, "coverage:\n")
  
  factor_levels <- levels(factor(X_factor[[var_name]]))   # citizenship is numeric in X, so take its levels from the values
  mapping_codes <- mapping$original_code
  
  missing_in_mapping <- setdiff(factor_levels, mapping_codes)
  extra_in_mapping <- setdiff(mapping_codes, factor_levels)
  
  if (length(missing_in_mapping) == 0 && length(extra_in_mapping) == 0) {
    cat("  OK Perfect coverage\n")
    result <- TRUE
  } else {
    if (length(missing_in_mapping) > 0) {
      cat("  X Missing from mapping:", length(missing_in_mapping), "codes\n")
    }
    if (length(extra_in_mapping) > 0) {
      cat("  X Extra in mapping:", length(extra_in_mapping), "codes\n")
    }
    result <- FALSE
  }
  
  return(result)
}

# Test 6: Check uniqueness
test_uniqueness <- function(mapping, name) {
  cat("\nTest 6 -", name, "uniqueness:\n")
  
  dup_original <- sum(duplicated(mapping$original_code))
  dup_new <- sum(duplicated(mapping$new_code))
  
  if (dup_original == 0 && dup_new == 0) {
    cat("  OK No duplicate codes\n")
    result <- TRUE
  } else {
    if (dup_original > 0) {
      cat("  X FAILED:", dup_original, "duplicate original_codes\n")
    }
    if (dup_new > 0) {
      cat("  X FAILED:", dup_new, "duplicate new_codes\n")
    }
    result <- FALSE
  }
  
  return(result)
}

# Combined test function
test_all <- function(mapping, X_factor, X_numeric, Y, var_name, name) {
  cat("\n")
  cat(strrep("=", 60), "\n")
  cat("TESTING:", name, "\n")
  cat(strrep("=", 60), "\n")
  
  results <- list(
    structure = test_mapping_structure(mapping, name),
    nas = test_mapping_nas(mapping, name),
    sequential = test_sequential_codes(mapping, name),
    wage_order = test_wage_ordering(X_numeric, Y, var_name, name),
    coverage = test_mapping_coverage(X_factor, mapping, var_name, name),
    uniqueness = test_uniqueness(mapping, name)
  )
  
  all_pass <- all(unlist(results))
  
  cat("\n")
  if (all_pass) {
    cat("  *** ALL TESTS PASSED ***\n")
  } else {
    cat("  !!  SOME TESTS FAILED OR HAVE WARNINGS !! \n")
  }
  
  return(results)
}

# Run tests on all mappings

# Plot mean wages by new code for each variable
plot_wage_by_code <- function(X_numeric, Y, var_name, title) {
  mean_wages <- tapply(Y, X_numeric[[var_name]], mean)
  plot(mean_wages, 
       xlab = "New Code", 
       ylab = "Mean Log Wage",
       main = title,
       pch = 19,
       col = "steelblue",
       type = "b")
  grid()
}

plot_wage_by_code(X_ordered_numeric, Y, "citizenship", "Citizenship")
plot_wage_by_code(X_ordered_numeric, Y, "marital", "Marital Status")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
